Okay, and they may be right. They may not have any enemies as such. There may not be any direct competitors who are actually in their markets at that time. But you can't just look at those folks. You have to look at the future as well. I'm going to digress for just a second because I've got a great example. Once upon a time, there was a person who could say with absolute conviction and certainty that he had no competition. He was, his name was Mark. I won't give last names. And he was the founder of Netscape. Netscape was the very first internet browser. It was the program that you used to surf the internet. If you were on the internet in the early to mid-1990s, when the internet first became commercially known, Netscape was your browser. It was what you used to access websites and look at things that were going on online. Okay? You know, in 1996, this gentleman, Mark, could honestly say with a straight face that he had no competition. In 1996, he had 98.7% of the market for internet browsers. There were one or two sort of specialized mom and pop products that were out there, but he had the market all to himself. He looked in this box and he could say, honestly, there's nobody there. But he overlooked somebody. Somebody who lives in Seattle, Washington, actually Redmond, near Mount Rainier, who even back then was the world's richest human being, who had the money and the resources to get into any kind of computer-related business that he bloody well wanted to. And who am I talking about? Bill Gates, Microsoft Corporation. Okay? Back then, Microsoft was the 800-pound gorilla in the software business. He took a look at this situation, Bill Gates did, and he said, you know what? This is a problem. The internet is the future here, and we don't have a product going on here. We need to get a browser product, and Netscape has 98% of the market. That's going to be a tough, tough row to hoe. So what he did was he developed his own product, or I think he bought it. I'm not really sure. Internet Explorer. Some of you know it. Some of you use Internet Explorer here. How many people here use Internet Explorer? Quite a few of you do. Okay? He launched his product in 1997, and he did something totally, utterly ruthless. He violated the antitrust laws of the United States. He did. He basically told all the developers who at the time were installing Windows software on people's computers, if you're going to install the next version of Windows on somebody's computer, you must carry Internet Explorer as the internet browser. Okay? You can let people disable it, but you've got to carry it along as part of the package. That violates the federal antitrust laws. That's called a tying arrangement.

file: Starting a Small Business, Part 3 . Dealing With Competition & Building Your Competitive Strategy.txt
text: You cannot force people to buy one product in order to buy another more desirable product. You can't lump your, you can offer packages. You certainly can do that. But you cannot say, to buy my desirable product, you must also buy this undesirable product. That violates the antitrust laws. Now, why did he do this? Was he stupid? Did he not know what he was doing? Of course not. Microsoft, even then, could afford the best lawyers in the world. He knew that he was in trouble here with violation. And he knew he was the government was going to come after him. But his attitude back at the time was, you know what? I've got to build the market for Microsoft. I don't care if the government comes after me. I've got the best lawyers in the world. I've got billions of dollars to play with here. I'll fight the battle. We'll drag it on in court for years. I'll probably get hit with a fine or some kind of a settlement. But by then, we will have established the market for Internet Explorer. And it certainly worked out. Three years later, in 1999, he settled with the Justice Department for something like, I want to say it was a couple of hundred million dollars or something, which for Microsoft is like, you know, that's a drop in the bucket. But by 1999, he had 60-some odd percent of the market for Internet browsers. Netscape was no longer a player in the marketplace, because Microsoft just beat the garbage out of him. It's basically what happened. Now, talk about ruthlessness in business, right? You know, how many of you here would take on the federal government to establish a market for your brand and beat the competition? Okay? But that's one of the most ruthless examples that I can think of, of what happens here. And it is accurate. Okay? So that's the thing. So very often, you don't have any enemies, but there's other people out there that you have to take into account. Okay? The second type of competitor, an indirect competitor, someone who's not doing the same thing that you are, but that are actually in the marketplace today, we refer to them as a substitute. Like the old Who song, substitute. A substitute is something that people can buy if for some reason your product or service is not desirable. A good way to find substitutes is to ask yourself the following question. If people could not afford my product or service, what other less expensive alternatives can they find that will deal with that particular fear or passion? That's a good way to find substitutes. Substitutes are usually people that operate cheaper than you do. You know, so for example, if you can't afford to hire a consultant to help you with your next job interview, you can buy my legal job interview book and spend $19.95. That's a good example of a substitute. If you don't have butter on hand to bake something with, you can use margarine. You know, if you are in the mood for pizza and there's no pizza place within driving distance, the Chinese takeout place across the street is right there. That's what a substitute is all about. Whenever for some reason someone can't or won't buy your product or service, what other more attractive alternatives are there out there that will satisfy the same fear, the same passion, the same need, if you will, that the marketplace is feeling. That's how you identify a substitute. And every business usually has substitutes of one kind or another. Okay, now let's go to box three. A potential competitor, somebody who's bigger than us, not on the market yet, but if they did come in, they would be a direct competitor and they would blow us off the map. Well, I'm just going to write the word big box in here because I want to get across the point that it's somebody, it's not just everybody, it's someone whose way of operation has economies of scale that we cannot match no matter what we do. So if you're a small hardware store, Lowe's and Home Depot. If you're an Italian restaurant, Sabaro's, Bertucci's, one of the big Italian chains.

file: Starting a Small Business, Part 3 . Dealing With Competition & Building Your Competitive Strategy.txt
text: Anybody that's bigger than you are, chain store, franchise, anybody that's operating at a different level and offering a broader variety of services for much lower prices is, should be in this box, even if they're not in your, in your, in your space quite yet. Okay. Now that leaves us with this last box here, box four. The indirect competitors of the future. Are these, are we getting out of, are we leaving terra firma here? Are we living, are we leaving the ground here and flying in the air here? You know, have we left the, the, the, the Mars, have we left Mars and the, and the asteroid belt? Are we now flying around the rings of Uranus and Neptune or someplace like that? Okay. The answer is no. The people who live in this box may well be your most compelling, compelling competitors. In fact, I will share with you that back around 10, 12 years ago, I sold my desktop publishing company to a much larger company because I saw what was coming in this box, and I didn't like what I saw. It was sometimes these people here are the people that can put you out of business. Okay. A hundred years ago, 1900, actually a little bit more than that, 1900, there were at least two dozen companies in the United States that made saddles, bridles, bits, and other horse related accessories, things that you, you need to buy when you have a horse. Obviously, the automobile. The car came along. Right. If you had a horse in 1900, it was how you got to and from work every morning. If you had a horse in 2000, a hundred years later, it was a very expensive hobby for very rich people. That was it. That was the difference. The people who live in this box, and sometimes it's not people, sometimes it's a thing, not a person, or a company. The people who live in this box are the people or things or technologies that are going to be making your products and services obsolete. That's the people who live in these boxes here. So, for example, in 19, you know, in 2001, when I was running my desktop publishing company, remember, I was publishing books, audio cassette programs, I was doing CDs, you know, the physical things, the physical discs, right? I saw the Internet coming along, and I said, you know what? This thing is going to clobber me. You know, I saw this coming, and I realized I was not the Internet entrepreneur that could bring this business into the 21st century, so I sold my business out to a company that could do that. Exactly. Sometimes the people who live in this box force you out of business when you see technology. We live in an age of great technology change. I'll be honest with you. I mean, I've been around. We're living in the middle of one of the great technology revolutions in human history. It began around 1978, 79, 1980, you know, about 35 years ago, and it's continuing today. Back in 1980, when the first PCs came out to today. People started leaving farms and working in factories. I see this as big a historical shift as the industrial revolution of the 1800s.

file: Starting a Small Business, Part 3 . Dealing With Competition & Building Your Competitive Strategy.txt
text: We are not going to come out of this the same people we were going in, and it's still going on now with artificial intelligence, voice recognition software, cars that drive themselves, electric cars. By the way, also, there's another reason why you should spend a lot of time looking at this box, because very often the people who live in these boxes, in this box, they are not just competitors, but they may be opportunities as well. They developed the technology that enabled them to survive and grow and morph into a technology company. Sometimes what lives in this box can be an opportunity as well as a threat, and you have to look at it that way. These are the four types of competitors. Anybody that does not live in one of these boxes is not a competitor. And by the way, it's not impossible that you might look at all four of these boxes and say, oh, my God, I don't see anybody. I don't see anybody in these four boxes. And it's not for one of looking. I really don't see anybody here, Cliff. I really am not just saying this to make you feel good. I really have looked, and I don't really see anybody. We've got some cutting-edge stuff going on here. There's nobody out there doing anything like what we're doing here. If that is truly your analysis and if you are right, first of all, there's a good chance you've missed somebody because you haven't been. See, this is where being neurotic helps. Remember we talked about that, being insecure in business? When you're neurotic, you see competitors behind every bush, you know, whether they exist or not. And that's a good thing. That's a good place to be. That's what keeps you going. That's what keeps the bad guys from killing you and taking you over, the insecure rabbit living longest. That's what I was talking about there. text: You don't see anybody on the racetrack because you're so far ahead of everybody else that there's nobody out there that's like you. text: Why are you going to beat all these other companies that are out there doing this stuff?
